01.note: Agra, the father-in-law of Rabbi Abba, found that in his phylacteries the leg of the letter heh in the word "the nation" had been cut off by a small hole in the parchment. He went to his son-in-law Rabbi Abba to ask whether they were still usable. Rabbi Abba told him that if the part of the leg still attached to the top of the letter was as long as a small letter, they were fit; if not, they were unfit.
01.why: The Gemara has just reported a ruling in Rav Yehuda's name that a heh whose leg is perforated is fit only if a small letter's length remains; this case shows the ruling applied in practice.

people.name: Agra
people.about: Rabbi Abba's father-in-law, whose phylacteries had a damaged letter

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Agra's son-in-law, whom Agra asked for a ruling

02.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that when Moses went up on High he found God tying little crowns onto the letters of the Torah. God explained that a man named Akiva ben Yosef would one day derive heaps of laws from every stroke of them. Moses asked to see him, sat at the back of Rabbi Akiva's study hall, understood nothing and lost heart, until a student asked Rabbi Akiva for his source and he answered that it was a law given to Moses at Sinai, which put Moses at ease. Moses asked why God would give the Torah through him and not this man, and then asked to see Akiva's reward; he saw Akiva's flesh being weighed in a butcher shop. To each protest God said: Be silent; this is what arose in My thought.
02.why: The Gemara has been discussing how exactly the letters of phylacteries and mezuzot must be formed; this story about the crowns on the letters leads into Rava's list of which letters need crowns and how scribes shaped them.

03.note: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri tells that some of his untithed produce once got mixed into a larger amount of produce that had already been tithed. He went to ask Rabbi Tarfon what to do. Rabbi Tarfon told him to go buy produce in the market, which may or may not have been tithed, and to separate the tithes from that produce on behalf of the mixture.
03.why: The Gemara has been listing rulings of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri; after this one it explains Rabbi Tarfon's reasoning, which turns on whether by Torah law the small amount of untithed produce is cancelled out in the larger mixture.

people.about: Tells this story about his own produce

people.about: The Sage whom Rabbi Shimon Shezuri asked for a ruling

terms.meaning: Crops from which the required portions for priests, Levites and the poor have not yet been set aside, and so may not be eaten.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

04.note: Rabbi Helbo reports that he saw Rav Huna roll up a mezuza from its last word back toward its first, and write its two passages in the "closed" style, with the second passage starting on the same line where the first ended. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who reports that Rabbi Meir wrote a mezuza on the inner layer of hide, shaped like a narrow column, with space above and below, and in the "open" style, starting the second passage on a new line. When he asked his teacher why, Rabbi Meir said it was because the two passages are not next to each other in the Torah.
04.why: The Gemara is working through how a mezuza must be laid out; Rav Huna's practice is challenged by Rabbi Meir's, and the Gemara goes on to ask which one Rav's ruling follows, settling that custom now favors the closed style.

05.note: Rav Helbo reports that he saw Rav Huna about to sit on his bed while a Torah scroll lay on it. Rav Huna first turned a jug upside down on the ground, set the Torah scroll on it, and only then sat on the bed.
05.why: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna held it forbidden to sit on a bed with a Torah scroll on it, and then notes that this disagrees with Rabbi Yohanan, who permits it.

06.note: Rabbi Yehuda reports that a student of Rabbi Akiva used to tie his phylacteries with strips of sky-blue wool instead of leather, and Rabbi Akiva said nothing to him. Someone asked whether that righteous man could really have seen his student do this and not object. Another Sage answered: yes, it could be that the student was wrong, because Rabbi Akiva never saw him; had he seen it, he would not have allowed it.
06.why: The Gemara quotes this from a baraita that requires phylacteries to be tied only with straps of hide; it is raised as an objection to Rabbi Yitzhak's ruling that the straps must be black.

07.note: Hyrcanus, the son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, used to tie his phylacteries with strips of purple wool, and his father said nothing to him. Someone asked whether that righteous man could have seen his son do this and not object. The Sages answered: yes, it could be that the son was wrong, because Rabbi Eliezer never saw him; had he seen it, he would not have allowed it.
07.why: This is the second incident in a baraita teaching that phylacteries must be tied with straps of hide; the Gemara raises the baraita against Rabbi Yitzhak's ruling that straps must be black, and answers that the black is required on the outside.

08.note: The Sage Peleimu asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on which head a man with two heads should put his phylacteries. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him either to go into exile or accept excommunication for such a question. Just then a man arrived saying a firstborn son with two heads had been born to him, and asked how much he must give the priest to redeem him. An elder came and told him he had to give ten sela, five for each head.
08.why: The Gemara has been asking where on the head phylacteries go; afterwards it questions the elder's ruling, since a child unlikely to live is normally not redeemed, and answers that the verse ties the redemption to each skull.

09.note: Ravina was walking behind Mar bar Rav Ashi on the Shabbat of a Festival when the corner of Mar bar Rav Ashi's garment, where one of his ritual fringes hung, tore off. Ravina said nothing until they reached Mar bar Rav Ashi's house, and then told him it had torn back on the road. Mar bar Rav Ashi said that if Ravina had told him there, he would have thrown the garment off right there.
09.why: The Gemara has just said the law does not follow Rabbi Yishmael, who held each fringe stands alone; this incident shows a garment missing one fringe treated as unfit to wear outdoors on Shabbat. The Gemara then asks why human dignity did not permit it.

people.name: Ravina

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Whose garment tore; said he would have thrown it off

terms.meaning: Strings tied to each of the four corners of a garment, as the Torah commands; if one corner lacks them, the garment does not fulfill the commandment.
A Sabbath during a festival, when carrying in a public place is forbidden.

10.note: In another version of what happened to Mar bar Rav Ashi's garment, Ravina told him about the torn corner right there on the road. Mar bar Rav Ashi answered: What do you think, that I should throw it off? Doesn't the Master say that human dignity is so great that it overrides a prohibition of the Torah?
10.why: The Gemara objects that this rule about dignity was said only of rabbinic prohibitions, and answers that where they were walking was a karmelit, an area where carrying is forbidden only by rabbinic law, so dignity allowed him to keep the garment on.

10.flag: The first STORY segment is the tail of the Gemara's answer to the previous story (Rav bar Shabba's interpretation), not part of the alternative version that follows.

11.note: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana were sitting together when a man passed by wearing a cloak made entirely of sky-blue wool, with fringes that were wound all the way down, with no loose strings hanging. Rav said the cloak was beautiful but the fringes were not. Rabba bar bar Hana said both the cloak and the fringes were beautiful.
11.why: The Gemara has been describing how the windings of the fringes must be made; it explains that the two Sages disagree over whether the verses allow fringes made only of windings, or whether loose strings must also hang from them.

people.about: Said the fully wound fringes were not beautiful

12.note: Rabba bar Huna visited Rava bar Rav Nahman and saw him wearing a cloak folded in half, with fringes tied at the corners of the fold. The cloak unfolded and the fringe ended up near his head, in the middle of the cloak. Rabba bar Huna told him this was not the corner the Torah speaks of. Rava bar Rav Nahman threw the cloak off and put on a different one. Rabba bar Huna then told him that fringes are not a duty on the man but on every cloak he owns, so he should go and put fringes on it properly.
12.why: The Gemara has just discussed whether a folded cloak needs fringes at its fold; this case raises the wider question of whether fringes are a duty of the person or of the garment, which the Gemara goes on to test.

people.about: Visitor who pointed out the misplaced fringe

people.name: Rava bar Rav Nahman
people.about: His host, who wore the folded cloak

terms.meaning: Strings the Torah commands to be tied to each of the four corners of a garment.

13.note: An angel found Rav Ketina wearing a linen cloak and said to him: Ketina, Ketina! A linen cloak in summer and a two-cornered coat in winter, garments that both need no fringes. What will become of the sky-blue fringes? Rav Ketina asked whether they punish even for failing to do a positive commandment. The angel answered that at a time of divine anger, they do punish.
13.why: The Gemara says the angel's words disagree with Rabba bar Huna, who held that fringes are a duty on every garment owned; it then argues over what the angel's rebuke shows, concluding he was charging Rav Ketina with looking for ways to avoid the commandment.

people.name: Rav Ketina
people.about: A Sage who wore garments exempt from fringes

people.name: an angel
people.about: Rebuked Rav Ketina for avoiding the commandment of fringes

14.note: Ravina and Rav Samma were sitting before Rav Ashi. Rav Samma saw that the corner of Ravina's cloak had torn, leaving the hole for the fringes closer to the edge than a thumb joint, and asked whether Ravina did not follow Rabbi Ya'akov's ruling. Ravina answered that the distance is required only when the fringes are made. Rav Samma was embarrassed, and Rav Ashi told him not to be upset: one of them is like two of us.
14.why: The Gemara has just explained why both Rav Pappa's and Rabbi Ya'akov's rulings on where to put the fringe hole are needed; this exchange clarifies that Rabbi Ya'akov's minimum distance applies when the fringes are attached, not after a later tear.

15.note: In the time of Rav Ahai, Mar from Mashkhei brought some sky-blue wool. It was tested by Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda's method and its color faded, then by Rav Adda's method and its color improved. The Sages thought to declare it unfit. Rav Ahai told them it cannot be neither true blue dye nor indigo; so the two tests must have been stated together, as one procedure.
15.why: The Gemara has just quoted two separate tests for real sky-blue dye; this case shows they can disagree, and Rav Ahai's conclusion turns them into two steps of one test, which word from the Land of Israel later confirms.

people.name: Rav Ahai

terms.meaning: The true sky-blue dye required for ritual fringes, taken from a sea creature; cheaper indigo looks the same.

16.note: A man careful about ritual fringes paid a prostitute overseas four hundred gold coins. She laid out seven beds, and sat naked on the top one. As he climbed up to join her, his four fringes struck him on the face, and he dropped to the ground; so did she, and she swore not to let him go until he told her what defect he saw in her. He swore she was the most beautiful woman he had seen, but the fringes appeared to him like four witnesses against him. She had him write down his name, city, teacher and study hall, divided up her property, and came to Rabbi Hiyya asking to convert. When he asked if she had her eye on a student, she showed him the note, and he told her to go take her purchase. The beds she had spread for him forbiddenly she now spread for him permitted.
16.why: Rabbi Natan has just taught that every commandment in the Torah carries a reward in this world, with the reward in the World-to-Come unknown; this story is his proof, and it closes by repeating that point.

17.note: Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that a man named Hanina ben Hizkiyya should be remembered for good, because without him the book of Ezekiel would have been withdrawn, since parts of it seemed to contradict the Torah. He carried three hundred jugs of oil up to his upper room, sat there, and interpreted the book until the contradictions were resolved.
17.why: The Gemara has been working through verses in Ezekiel that seem to clash with Torah law about offerings; this statement closes that discussion.

18.note: The Sages told Rabbi Perida that Rabbi Ezra, a man of famous lineage, descended from Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and from Ezra the Scribe, was waiting at his gate. Rabbi Perida asked why all the detail: a man of Torah is worthy to enter, but a man of lineage without Torah, let fire devour him. They said Rabbi Ezra was a man of Torah, so he let him in. Seeing his guest was upset, Rabbi Perida offered a teaching on a psalm in which God gives credit only to the Patriarchs, using the word "addir". Rabbi Ezra picked up the word and replied with his own wordplay on addir and yadid, about God punishing the Egyptians in the sea.
18.why: The Gemara has just reported a question Rabbi Perida put to Rabbi Ami about meal offerings, and moves on to an incident involving the same Rabbi Perida.

19.note: During a civil war between Hasmonean kings, Hyrcanus besieged Jerusalem from outside and Aristoblus held it from inside. Each day those inside let down coins in a box and those outside sent up animals for the daily offerings. An old man who knew Greek wisdom told the besiegers in coded language that as long as the Temple service went on, the city would not fall to them. The next day they sent up a pig. When it reached halfway up the wall it dug its hooves in, and the Land of Israel shook for four hundred parasangs in each direction. Then the Sages said: Cursed is he who raises pigs, and cursed is he who teaches his son Greek wisdom.
19.why: The mishna mentions that once the omer barley came from Gaggot Tzerifin, far from Jerusalem; this baraita explains that it happened in this war, when the fields near the city were ruined.

20.note: When it was time to bring the omer, no one knew where to find barley for it, so it was announced publicly. A deaf-mute came and put one hand on a roof and the other on a hut. Mordekhai asked whether there was a place called Gaggot Tzerifin, which means "roofs of huts". They checked and found it.
20.why: The mishna records that the omer once came from Gaggot Tzerifin; the Gemara has told how war ruined the fields near Jerusalem, and this tradition tells how the distant place was found.
